title: Other people's faults (244–255)
hook: others' faults are easy to see, our own hard; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own (Dhammapada 252)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smith and the silver: dross blown off one by one. Your line was little by little. What small thing did you polish? Day two hundred six.

Riding in the passenger seat, you can see every mistake the driver makes. Too close. Too fast. Missed the exit. You could write a report. Then you get behind the wheel yourself, and somehow all your own habits disappear from view. Or listen to a friend describe her sister: every flaw laid out in perfect detail. Ask her for her own three biggest flaws, and there's a long pause. Everyone has a perfect view of other people and a blind spot the size of a truck about themselves. Chapter eighteen names it exactly. Today: other people's faults.
screen: `THE PASSENGER SEES EVERYTHING.` → `BEHIND THE WHEEL, NOTHING.` → `A BLIND SPOT THE SIZE OF A TRUCK.`

segments.voice: Verse two fifty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler." Two pictures in one verse. First, winnowing. At harvest, farmers tossed grain up into the wind so the light chaff would blow away. Picture someone tossing another person's faults high into the air, for everyone to see, scattering them across the whole village. Second, a cheat at dice, palming the loaded die so no one notices it. That's what we do with our own. The Pali word for fault here is vajja, something to be avoided, something blameworthy. And the next verse warns what happens to the fault-finder. Verse two fifty-three: "If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow". The irony is sharp. Constant judging doesn't make you better. It feeds the very things you're judging. The chapter gathers a few more pictures before it ends. Verse two fifty-one: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed." And a reminder that a person isn't made holy by outward show, which is where tomorrow's chapter picks up. None of this says other people have no faults. It says the eye that sees theirs so clearly would do its best work turned around.
screen: `WINNOWING SOMEONE ELSE'S CHAFF.` · `THE CHEAT HIDES THE BAD DIE.` · `JUDGING FEEDS WHAT IT JUDGES.` · `NO SHARK LIKE HATRED.` · then, large: `EASY TO SEE OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone whose faults you know by heart. Name one of them silently. Now, gently, turn the same bright light around. Is there any trace of that fault in you? Not to punish yourself. Just to look, the way you'd check your own mirror. Often there's a small echo. If there is, simply see it: oh, there it is. If there isn't, look for the fault you'd least like anyone to see. Then set it down, and let the breath be plain and open. The bell holds the time.
Other people's faults. Verse two fifty-two: easy to see, while our own are hard to see; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own.
Your line: easy to see others. Today, catch yourself judging once, and before you finish the thought, ask where that fault lives in you. Day two hundred six.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics regularly confess their own faults to one another, and teachers often cite verse 252 to turn attention from criticizing others to examining oneself.

fork.setup: a coworker keeps interrupting in meetings, and you've noticed every single time. what would verse 252 have you look at?
options: keep a list of every interruption.
whether you have a fault you're hiding like a bad die.
fork.reveal: others' faults are easy to winnow in the wind; our own we hide "as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler."

original.note: Pali: a fault, something to be avoided — sudassaṃ vajjam aññesaṃ, others' faults are easy to see.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be judgmental.
what it means: we see others' faults clearly and hide our own, and constant fault-finding only feeds our own passions.
what a scholar hears: verse 252 pairs two images: winnowing (opuṇāti) the chaff of others' faults and hiding one's own like a crooked gambler hides the losing throw.
